title: Sole Proprietorship Structure and Liability
context: Analyze the defining features of a sole proprietorship as a form of business ownership. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A sole proprietorship is owned by one person who also manages and runs the business.
The sole proprietorship is not a legal entity of its own, so profits are reported on the owner's personal income tax statement.
A sole proprietor enjoys limited liability so private assets stay fully protected if business debts cannot be repaid.
Sole proprietorships require substantial minimum share capital before trading may begin.
Hiring staff removes the sole proprietor from responsibility for major management decisions and business risk.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Ownership and day-to-day management rest with a single proprietor.
TRUE — Without separate legal personality, profits are taxed as the owner's personal income.
FALSE — The sole proprietor has unlimited liability; private assets are also at stake.
FALSE — Sole proprietorships are easy to establish and face no such capital requirement.
FALSE — Even with hired personnel, the proprietor retains key decisions and bears the risk.

title: Partnership Agreement and Partner Liability
context: Consider two consultants who jointly found a business and draft a partnership agreement covering ownership shares, profit division, and decision rights. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A partnership is formed when two or more persons jointly found a business and settle rights in a partnership agreement.
In a general partnership all partners typically share equal rights, liabilities, and responsibilities.
Each general partner is solely liable for all debts of the business under unlimited liability.
A limited partner who does not manage the business still carries unlimited liability for all partnership debts.
Partners cannot specialise in different tasks because every partner must perform identical management duties.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Joint founding plus a partnership agreement defines the partnership structure.
TRUE — General partnerships assign equal rights, liabilities, and responsibilities to partners.
TRUE — Unlimited liability means each general partner can be held for the whole debt.
FALSE — In a limited partnership, a limited partner's liability is capped at the capital contributed.
FALSE — Partners may share tasks and specialise while remaining jointly responsible.

title: Corporations as Legal Entities
context: Review how corporations differ from unincorporated businesses through separate legal personality and limited shareholder liability. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A corporation is a legal entity of its own and can own property, hire people, close contracts, sue, and be sued.
Shareholders need not manage the corporation, and managers need not own shares of the business.
Shareholders' liability is usually limited to the amount they invested when buying the shares.
Share capital is divided into shares so that large sums can be raised when investors purchase stock.
Once share prices rise on the stock exchange after issue, the issuing corporation automatically receives additional financing equal to that price rise.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Corporations are legal persons with the same rights and obligations as natural persons in business life.
TRUE — Ownership and management can be separated in a corporation.
TRUE — Limited liability confines shareholders' exposure to their invested capital.
TRUE — Selling shares builds share capital that finances the corporation.
FALSE — Post-issue market gains accrue to shareholders; they do not inject new funds into the issuer.

title: Unincorporated versus Incorporated Ownership
context: Analyze the overview that distinguishes unincorporated from incorporated forms of business ownership. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Unincorporated businesses are not legal entities of their own, whereas incorporated businesses are legal persons.
In unincorporated forms such as sole proprietorships and partnerships, owners and managers are typically the same persons.
In corporations, owners and managers need not be the same persons because shareholders provide capital and directors run the company.
A sole proprietorship is classified as an incorporated business because it files personal income tax on profits.
Limited liability companies belong with unincorporated businesses because their shares are not always listed on a stock exchange.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Separate legal personality is the core split between unincorporated and incorporated structures.
TRUE — Sole traders and partners usually both own and manage the firm.
TRUE — Corporate structure allows shareholders to own while directors manage.
FALSE — A sole proprietorship remains unincorporated and lacks separate legal personality.
FALSE — Private limited companies are still incorporated legal persons with limited liability.

title: Equity Finance and Debt Finance
context: Review the main sources of finance available to businesses as classified into equity and debt. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Share capital provided by investors is an external equity source of finance for corporations.
Retained earnings that are reinvested in the business are an internal equity source of finance.
Bank overdrafts and trade credit are examples of short-term debt finance.
Long-term bank loans and bonds issued to investors are forms of long-term debt finance.
Debt finance is classified as internal finance because interest payments return profit to the owners.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Share capital comes from outside investors and counts as equity finance.
TRUE — Profits retained in the firm supply internal equity finance without interest charges.
TRUE — Overdrafts and supplier trade credit finance short-term obligations as debt.
TRUE — Loans and bonds provide longer-term creditors' funds that must be repaid with interest.
FALSE — Debt finance is external; interest is a cost of borrowing, not internal equity.

title: Share Markets, Dividends and Corporate Bonds
context: Analyze how share demand, dividends, voting rights, and bond issues relate to corporation finance after shares have already been issued. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Comparatively low interest rates tend to support higher demand for shares because alternative fixed-return investments become less attractive.
A corporation that withholds dividends for a long period may face weaker investor demand and falling share prices even though dividend payments remain discretionary.
Holders of preferred shares usually forgo voting rights at the stockholders' meeting in exchange for a higher dividend claim.
Issuing bonds can be attractive because the interest rate on bonds is often lower than the interest rate on a comparable bank loan.
If secondary-market share prices rise after the IPO, the corporation records matching equity finance equal to the cumulative market gain.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Lower interest rates reduce the relative appeal of interest-bearing alternatives and can raise share demand.
TRUE — Dividends are not obligatory, yet prolonged non-payment can make shares unattractive and pressure prices.
TRUE — Preferred stock typically trades voting rights for preferential dividend treatment.
TRUE — Bond issues may finance large projects more cheaply than bank borrowing.
FALSE — Secondary price rises benefit trading shareholders; they do not inject additional share capital into the issuer.

title: Matching Finance to Use Cost and Gearing
context: Consider a manufacturer that already carries a high proportion of loan capital and must choose how to fund a multi-year production plant versus routine materials purchases. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Capital expenditures on assets used over many years should normally be matched with long-term finance.
Revenue expenditures such as buying materials for current production can safely be financed by short-term sources.
A highly geared business may struggle to raise further credit except at higher interest rates and/or against additional collateral.
When loan capital is already high, internal funds or new equity investors can reduce insolvency risk relative to taking another large loan.
The only relevant criterion when choosing a source of finance is the absolute interest rate, so matching term to asset life and gearing risk can be ignored.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Long-lived asset spending calls for long-term finance so repayment timing matches use.
TRUE — Short-cycle materials need short-term credit such as overdrafts or trade credit.
TRUE — High gearing makes lenders cautious and often raises the price or collateral demand of new debt.
TRUE — Extra debt increases repayment burden; retained earnings or investors avoid adding that load.
FALSE — Cost matters, but intended use and current gearing also shape the appropriate choice.
